Here in Quzhou, there is really only one way to farm — winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. My father did it, my neighbors do it, and so do I. The soil here is flat loam, good for these two crops. I have about 8 mu of contracted land.

For wheat, I'll plant in mid-October after getting the field rotary-tilled. I'll buy improved variety seed from the county co-op — probably 济麦22 or similar, whatever the extension station recommends this year. I broadcast compound fertilizer (nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium) as base before planting, then top-dress with urea in spring. I irrigate four times: once before freeze to protect roots, once when it greens up in March, once at jointing, once when the grain is filling. I spray twice — once for aphids in spring, once for powdery mildew if I see it.

Once wheat comes off in early June, I plant corn immediately — no time to waste. I use hybrid seed, always, because the yield difference is real. I do no-till direct seeding right into the stubble. I apply fertilizer in one shot with planting and maybe top-dress urea when the plant is knee-high. Summer rain usually handles irrigation but I'll run the pump once in August if it's dry. Corn doesn't need much pesticide here — maybe once for corn borer if I see egg masses.

I use improved wheat varieties from the local co-op and hybrid maize seed, apply compound base fertilizer plus urea topdressing at conventional rates, irrigate wheat four times to protect against drought stress at key growth stages, and rely on summer rainfall to cover most of maize water needs.
